query: Given a CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy where conventional casting yields porosity and a homogeneous but soft single-phase structure, and where previous attempts suffered from low hardness, propose a solid-state processing strategy involving high-energy milling followed by rapid sintering. The target is to suppress porosity while driving the formation of a fine-grained nanocrystalline solid solution (dominated by FCC with minor BCC) rather than a brittle HCP phase often associated with Titanium-rich systems. Incorporate known constraints on displacement rates and thermal expansion during sintering into the hypothesis. Define the operating regime (temperature/strain rate) where this dual-phase stability is maximized, and propose a specific mechanical test (e.g., indentation load and dwell time) that would falsify the claim that the observed hardness is due to grain refinement rather than solute strengthening.

generation.hypothesis: High-energy ball milling of CoCrFeNiTi elemental powders followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at a temperature just below the solidus (approx. 950°C) with a controlled displacement rate will suppress porosity and kinetically stabilize a fine-grained nanocrystalline FCC solid solution with a minor BCC phase, while suppressing the formation of brittle HCP Ti-rich phases that typically form during slow cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental powders of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti mixed in equiatomic ratios, exhibiting high surface energy and potential for cold welding, but prone to forming brittle intermetallics or HCP phases if thermally equilibrated slowly.
generation.intervention: High-energy ball milling (HEBM) for 10 hours to induce severe plastic deformation and amorphization, followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 950°C with a heating rate of 100°C/min and a holding time of 5 minutes under 50 MPa uniaxial pressure.
generation.conditions: Sintering temperature: 950°C (approx. 0.6 Tm); Heating rate: 100°C/min; Displacement rate: Controlled to maintain constant strain rate of ~10^-3 s^-1 during densification; Atmosphere: High vacuum (<10^-3 Pa) to prevent oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The high density of dislocations and grain boundaries introduced during milling acts as a kinetic trap, lowering the activation energy for nucleation of the FCC solid solution while raising the energy barrier for the diffusion-controlled transformation to HCP Ti-rich phases. The rapid thermal cycle of SPS limits grain growth and solute segregation.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical alloying creates a supersaturated solid solution with high defect density. During rapid SPS, the high heating rate and short dwell time prevent the thermodynamic driving force for HCP phase separation (which requires long-range diffusion of Ti) from being realized, favoring the metastable FCC/BCC nanocrystalline solid solution. The applied pressure ensures pore closure before significant grain coarsening occurs.
generation.predicted_outcome: A fully dense (>99.5%) nanocrystalline alloy with an average grain size of 20-50 nm, consisting of a dominant FCC matrix with 5-10% BCC precipitates, exhibiting a Vickers hardness of 450-550 HV, significantly higher than the cast counterpart, without the brittleness associated with HCP phases.
generation.baseline: Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi alloy with 2-5% porosity, a coarse-grained single-phase FCC structure, and a hardness of 150-200 HV.
generation.boundary: The strategy fails if the sintering temperature exceeds 1050°C (promoting HCP formation and grain growth) or if the milling time is insufficient (<10 hours) to achieve the necessary supersaturation and defect density. The process is also bounded by the melting point of Ti (~1668°C) and the eutectic temperatures of the system.
generation.uncertainty: There is a risk that the extreme strain rates during milling could induce local heating sufficient to trigger premature HCP nucleation, or that the rapid sintering might not fully eliminate porosity if the particle size distribution is too broad. The exact phase fraction of BCC is uncertain and may vary with minor stoichiometric deviations. While Ti addition generally increases hardness, the specific fraction of BCC vs FCC in this specific equiatomic system under rapid kinetics is not definitively established in the provided literature.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: Set A (milled for 10h + SPS at 950°C, 100°C/min) and Set B (milled for 10h + SPS at 950°C, 5°C/min heating rate, 2h dwell). Perform nanoindentation on both sets using a load of 10 mN and a dwell time of 10 seconds. Additionally, perform a separate test on Set A where the milling time is reduced to 2 hours.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Set B (slow sintering) shows a significant increase in HCP phase fraction and a decrease in hardness compared to Set A, the hypothesis that rapid kinetics suppress HCP is supported. However, if Set A (rapid sintering) shows no significant hardness increase over the baseline cast alloy despite grain refinement, or if the hardness increase correlates perfectly with the presence of HCP phases (detected by XRD) rather than grain size, the claim that hardness is due to grain refinement in a metastable FCC/BCC system is falsified. Specifically, if the hardness of the nanocrystalline sample is lower than the coarse-grained sample with the same phase composition, the Hall-Petch relationship is violated, falsifying the grain refinement mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
